questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The fact that the general language is English was important to me since it makes it much easier to get to know the locals at the university, chat with people and be integrated in your local communities. I have heard a lot about Edinburgh from friends and family, and they all recommended the city as well as the university. I wanted to experience some of the beautiful nature in the highlands surrounding the city, and it was important to me that it was easily accessible. Furthermore, previous exchange students had had good experiences at the university, and I was looking forward to study at a high ranking institution like The University of Edinburgh.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The university was very good at keeping one updated by mail, and they were quick to answer emails sent to them. Just make sure to check your email often, then you'll be guided through all the practical things you'll need to organize before going. However, one piece of information which was difficult to find, was an overview of all the courses exchange students were able to participate in. But if you look up
http://www.drps.ed.ac.uk
, which can be difficult to find through the official website, the details about the course are provided.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: You are assigned with a personal academic tutor, who is an academic member of staff who will help you, if you have any academic questions throughout the semester. The university arranged several small events, where international students could meet each other, such as picnics and parties.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it much harder than I expected, since I heard from other students that it was fairly easy. I began to search for off campus housing about 1,5 month before going, which was a little late. The university has a housing guarantee for interantional students, but this is only for those who are staying for one academic year or more. The short stay of one semester was also a problem when searching for off campus accomodation, since many landlords has a minimum stay of one year. I heard of other Erasmus students who lived in hostels weeks after they arrived to the city, but on a Facebook group I found hosuing through one, who had contact to several host families. I would recommend to start searching 1,5-2 months before going, and use your network, Facebook groups and the usual website such as gumtree or spareroom.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I had many experiences of Scottish culture, that my friends didn't have since they lived with other international students. The off campus accommodation is a unique opportunity to feel like a local by being integrated in the local community and to get to know some of the Scottish culture and history through your flatmates. My experience is, that this is definetely more difficult when living in university accommodation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Once I knew the webiste with all the courses the university provided, I found the enrollement pretty easy. Although the univerisity first knows what courses they provide in the first learning week, so you're only certain of what courses you are enrolled in when you arrive. I had contact with the Visiting Student Office by mail before i knew what courses I would apply for, but they were very helpful and quick to answer.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above the Visiting Student Office was there to help me, and by mailing back and forth during a period,  they helped me to apply for the courses. I also attended to an online session about the application process provided by the university, where a lot of beneficial information was provided and I had the opportunity the live chat with the staff.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted to apply for. The main problem for me was that the possibility to find courses which could replace the one's I had at my home university was limited.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask for help and email the visiting student office - the staff are there to help you. I was a bit hesitant to contact them at first, but you shouldn't be. And go to the information session, where you'll get an impression of what the city and university is like.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had three courses during my semester, which covered Clinical Psychology and Scientific Design and PhiloSophy of Science. Due to COVID all my lectures and some of the classes were unfortunately online. But I was a bit disappointed of how short some of the lectures were (15-20 minutes) even though my courses were 10 ECTS each. At the same time, most of the classes weren't as well structured as in Copenhagen, since they were based on plain student discussion, were the teacher didn't prepare any presentation, questions to the students or other material to work from.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was lower, since the courses generally covered more subjects than in Copenhagen, which meant that I didn't go as much into depth with each subject as I'm used to.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching was less teacher-led and more dependent on the students and their discussion.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Philosophy of Science 1
- Contemporary Issues in Health and Wellbeing 
- Psychological Perspectives on Health and Care

These courses covered Clinical Psychology and Scientific Design and PhiloSophy of Science on Copenhagen University.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Philosophy of Science 1 is great if you are into philosophy or want to know more about it. It was by far the best structured course I had, and it covered a lot of interesting topics.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs but make sure to have money for eating out and going out, and for travelling if you want to go on road trips in the Highlands or similar things.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were much cheaper than I expected, while the prices at restaurants were the same.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The student societies provide a huge amount of activities for students at the university. I was part of a hillwalking society, mountaineering society and a trail runner society, but there are societies for almost everything you can imagine. Most of the societies are described on the university's website.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the hillwalking club if you want to go to walk some hills in the Highlands. It's great fun, you'll see some stunning nature and meet other students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Some of the places I went to and was happy to see were Glasgow, Isle of Skye, Glencoe, Inverness and Loch Lomond. There is lots of very beautiful nature once you go a bit north!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: They can be very hard to understand at first, since their dialect is so strong. But you will get used to it pretty quickly. In general, I didn't find it hard to adjust to the local culture, and even though there are many differences between Scotland and Denmark, it is overall easy to chat with them and get to know them.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I think one of the best ways to get to know them, is by joining some student societies. Many of them are both having weekly events and arranging trips on the weekends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Understanding their language!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The folk music at the pubs. I recommend going to some of the small pubs where people are a bit older, since they often have a lot of great music and a nice atmosphere. But the Scots are also very talkative and open, so it is much easier to chat with them compared to the Danes.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Join a student society
2. Bring warm clothes, rainwear and hiking boots. The Scottish weather is hard to predict.
3. The application process can be long and difficult, but in the end, it will be worth it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Joining the student societies, exploring the Highlands and Scottish nature, meeting international students from both Europe and the rest of the world, to be in a beautiful and historically rich city, to be integrated into the local communities.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The exam period was tough with many exams following each other and with little time to do them. But all of them were finished before Christmas, so you have a long holiday in the winter if you go abroad in the autumn.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
